{{Short description|Encryption methods for TV programs}}
{{redirect|Revocation scheme|distrust of compromised certificates|certificate revocation}}
'''Broadcast encryption''' is the [[cryptography|cryptographic]] problem of delivering [[encryption|encrypted]] content (e.g. TV programs or data on DVDs) over a [[broadcasting|broadcast channel]] in such a way that only qualified users (e.g. subscribers who have paid their fees or DVD players conforming to a specification) can decrypt the content.<ref name="broadcast_encryption">{{cite book|author1=Amos Fiat|author2=Moni Naor|editor-last=Stinson|editor-first=Douglas R.|editor-link=Doug Stinson|chapter=Broadcast Encryption|type=Extended abstract|title=Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO' 93|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=773|pages=480–491|year=1994|chapter-url=http://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~naor/PAPERS/broad_abs.html|doi=10.1007/3-540-48329-2_40|doi-access=free|isbn=978-3-540-57766-9}}</ref><ref name="practical_sharing">{{cite conference|author1=Noam Kogan|author2=Yuval Shavitt|author3=Avishai Wool|title=A Practical Revocation Scheme for Broadcast Encryption Using Smart Cards|type=Extended abstract|conference=24th IEEE Symposium on Security & Privacy|date=May 2003}}</ref><ref name="combinatorial_bounds"/> The challenge arises from the requirement that the set of qualified users can change in each broadcast emission, and therefore revocation of individual users or user groups should be possible using broadcast transmissions, only, and without affecting any remaining users. As efficient revocation is the primary objective of broadcast encryption, solutions are also referred to as '''revocation schemes'''.<ref name="subset_cover">{{cite conference|author1=Dalit Naor|author2=Moni Naor|author-link2=Moni Naor|author3=Jeff Lotspiech|title=Revocation and Tracing Schemes for Stateless Receivers|book-title=Proc. Advances in Cryptology – CRYPTO '01|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=2139|pages=41–62|url =http://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~naor/PAPERS/2nl.html|doi =10.1007/3-540-44647-8_3|year=2001|isbn=3-540-42456-3|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="multi_revoke">{{cite book|author1=Scott C.-H. Huang|author2=Ding-Zhu Du |title=Proceedings IEEE 24th Annual Joint Conference of the IEEE Computer and Communications Societies |chapter=New constructions on broadcast encryption and key pre-distribution schemes |volume=1|pages=515–523|date=March 2005|doi=10.1109/INFCOM.2005.1497919|isbn=978-0-7803-8968-7|s2cid=17709190}}</ref><ref name="NewtonRevocation">{{cite conference|author1=Noam Kogan|author2=Tamir Tassa|title=Improved Efficiency for Revocation Schemes via Newton Interpolation|journal=ACM Transactions on Information and System Security|year=2006|volume=9|pages=461–486|url =https://www.openu.ac.il/lists/mediaserver_documents/personalsites/tamirtassa/nr.pdf}}</ref>

Rather than directly encrypting the content for qualified users, broadcast encryption schemes [[key distribution|distribute keying information]] that allows qualified users to reconstruct the content encryption key whereas revoked users find insufficient information to recover the key.<ref name="broadcast_encryption"/> The typical setting considered is that of a [[simplex communication|unidirectional]] broadcaster and stateless users (i.e., users do not keep bookmarking of previous messages by the broadcaster), which is especially challenging.<ref name="subset_cover"/> In contrast, the scenario where users are supported with a bi-directional communication link with the broadcaster and thus can more easily maintain their state, and where users are not only dynamically revoked but also added (joined), is often referred to as [[multicast encryption]].<ref name="multicast_encryption">{{cite conference|author1=Ran Canetti|author2=Tal Malkin|author2-link=Tal Malkin|author3=Kobbi Nissim|title=Efficient communication-storage tradeoffs for multicast encryption|book-title=Proc. Theory and application of cryptographic techniques – EUROCRYPT '99|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=1592|pages=459–474|year=1999|isbn=3-540-65889-0}}</ref>

The problem of practical broadcast encryption has first been formally studied by [[Amos Fiat]] and [[Moni Naor]] in 1994.<ref name="broadcast_encryption"/> Since then, several solutions have been described in the literature, including [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] constructions, one-time revocation schemes based on [[secret sharing]] techniques, and [[tree (data structure)|tree]]-based constructions.<ref name="practical_sharing"/> In general, they offer various trade-offs between the increase in the size of the broadcast, the number of keys that each user needs to store, and the feasibility of an unqualified user or a collusion of unqualified users being able to decrypt the content. [[Michael Luby|Luby]] and [[Jessica Staddon|Staddon]] have used a combinatorial approach to study the trade-offs for some general classes of broadcast encryption algorithms.<ref name="combinatorial_bounds">{{cite book|author1=Michael Luby|author2=Jessica Staddon|editor-last=Nyberg|editor-first=K.|title=Advances in Cryptology — EUROCRYPT'98 |chapter=Combinatorial bounds for broadcast encryption |author2-link=Jessica Staddon|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=1403|pages=512–526|year=1998|doi=10.1007/BFb0054150|doi-access=free|isbn=978-3-540-64518-4}}</ref> A particularly efficient tree-based construction is the "subset difference" scheme, which is derived from a class of so-called subset cover schemes.<ref name="subset_cover"/> The subset difference scheme is notably implemented in the [[Advanced Access Content System|AACS]] for [[HD DVD]] and [[Blu-ray]] Disc encryption. A rather simple broadcast encryption scheme is used for the [[Content Scramble System|CSS]] for [[DVD]] encryption.

The problem of rogue users sharing their decryption keys or the decrypted content with unqualified users is mathematically insoluble. ''[[Traitor tracing]]'' [[algorithm]]s aim to minimize the damage by retroactively identifying the user or users who leaked their keys, so that punitive measures, legal or otherwise, may be undertaken.<ref name="traitor_tracing">{{cite book|author1=Benny Chor|author1-link= Benny Chor |author2=Amos Fiat|author3=Moni Naor|chapter=Tracing traitors|title=Proc. Advances in Cryptology – CRYPTO '94|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=839|pages=257–270|year=1994|isbn=978-3-540-58333-2}}</ref><ref name="subset_cover"/> In practice, [[pay TV]] systems often  employ [[set-top box]]es with [[Tamper resistance|tamper-resistant]] [[smart card]]s that impose physical restraints on a user learning their own decryption keys. Some broadcast encryption schemes, such as AACS, also provide tracing capabilities.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aacsla.com/specifications/AACS_Spec_Common_FINAL_0951.pdf |title="AACS Specifications: Introduction and Common Cryptographic Elements Book" |access-date=2010-10-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100827031359/http://www.aacsla.com/specifications/AACS_Spec_Common_FINAL_0951.pdf |archive-date=2010-08-27 }}</ref>
